re:  
Comments of Chair of Virginia Energy Commission  
Dear Commissioners: 
I commend FERC for addressing governance issues at PJM and appreciate the opportunity to 
comment on this criƟcal issue aﬀecƟng our region.  I chair the Energy Commission of Virginia (formerly 
known as the Commission on Electric UƟlity RegulaƟon, or CEUR). The Energy Commission of Virginia is 
the standing legislaƟve commission established by the Virginia General Assembly to vet and discuss 
complex uƟlity issues on behalf of the General Assembly’s 140 members.  Our primary responsibility is to 
to report to the General Assembly and Governor on recommendaƟons to maintain reliable service in the 
Commonwealth while preserving the Commonwealth's posiƟon as a low-cost electricity market.  We 
cannot achieve either of these criƟcal standards without a highly funcƟoning regional electricity grid and 
energy market.  We appreciate the complex role that PJM serves as the RTO/ISO.   
If Governors are provided any kind of role or input into PJM governance, then state legislators 
should have equal access to engage meaningfully in the PJM decision-making and governance process, 
similar to the access provided to our state uƟlity regulators.  State legislators serve with disƟnct 
funcƟons, as a coequal branch under the ConsƟtuƟon of Virginia.  Both execuƟve and legislaƟve 
branches should have access to PJM regional governance processes given their independent powers. It is 
our understanding that governors have asked for a role in the PJM governance process.  If governors are

given a role, there should also be a means for state legislatures to parƟcipate, given that there is not 
always poliƟcal alignment between governors’ oﬃces and state legislatures.  
Virginia’s uƟlity regulator is the State CorporaƟon Commission, whose Judges of the Commission 
(“Commissioners”) are appointed through the legislaƟve branch. To ensure more eﬀecƟve coordinaƟon 
and address increasing challenges, I am fully supporƟve of granƟng more authority to the OrganizaƟon 
of PJM States, Inc. (OPSI) to ensure more eﬀecƟve load forecasƟng, PJM wholesale and capacity market 
condiƟons and beƩer transmission planning, to name a few key consideraƟons.  
Like my colleagues from the NaƟonal Caucus of Environmental Legislators (NCEL), I believe it is 
crucial that FERC prioriƟze reforms that ensure states can engage meaningfully in PJM governance and 
stakeholder processes and have access to suﬃcient informaƟon.  States have authority over essenƟal 
energy policy maƩers including siƟng, permiƫng, generaƟon and retail cost allocaƟon. It is imperaƟve 
for states to have a voice in the regional decisions PJM is making that aﬀect our state’s economy, health 
and safety, through transmission planning, energy markets, and resource adequacy.  
Like others in this process, I encourage FERC to review surrounding regions and build on the 
precedents and lessons learned from other bodies, such as the New England States CommiƩee on 
Electricity (NESCOE) and the Southwest Power Pool’s (SPP) Regional State CommiƩee (RSC). 
Virginia has greatly beneﬁted from the PJM regional compact, leveraging the region’s assets to 
help achieve energy reliability through access to the wholesale market.  There are numerous regional 
topics that should be addressed holisƟcally through the governance and stakeholder processes at PJM, 
including but not limited to load growth forecasts, inter-state transmission projects, and regional or 
state-based environmental goals, such as electric uƟlity decarbonizaƟon and renewable porƞolio 
standards. Having dedicated voice for legislaƟve perspecƟves in PJM governance will enhance regional 
progress to overcome the challenges of our Ɵme.   
I echo the recommendaƟons of NCEL and implore FERC to take acƟon on their recommendaƟons 
as follows: 
● Establish a formal governance role for a new or exisƟng organizaƟon represenƟng state 
interests, including legislators. This role could be based on the “direcƟon to ﬁle” and regional 
policy funcƟons exercised by state enƟƟes in other regions, such as the RSC in SPP or ISO-NE’s 
NESCOE. 
● Provide a seat on the NominaƟng CommiƩee for the PJM Board to a representaƟve from the 
states. 
● Modify the Board makeup requirements to provide two addiƟonal seats, including a seat to 
represent the interests of states and a seat to represent the interests of end-use customers.  
● Amend PJM’s foundaƟonal operaƟng agreement to codify an explicit public interest mandate 
that requires PJM to balance system reliability and market eﬃciency with public interest 
objecƟves.

● Strengthen transparency by allowing designated representaƟves of PJM state governments to 
aƩend Liaison CommiƩee meeƟngs. 
 
The pracƟcal modiﬁcaƟons and adjustments to the PJM stakeholder process, as oﬀered by NCEL, 
to ensure eﬀecƟve and transparent decision-making are good policy suggesƟons: 
● Record all PJM Stakeholder MeeƟngs and make these recordings publicly available.  
● Implement sector-weighted voƟng in the Standing CommiƩees to align commiƩee work with 
the ulƟmate stakeholder decision-making process. 
● Publish and disseminate records of voƟng results taken in all PJM commiƩees, task forces, and 
similar standing, ad-hoc, or issue-speciﬁc stakeholder groups. 
● Allow media to be present in all stakeholder process meeƟngs. 
● Require cost impact analyses to be presented during the First Read at the Senior Standing 
CommiƩees. 
 
These governance reforms would help ensure that PJM's decision-making beƩer reﬂects the 
prioriƟes of the states it serves, while bringing more transparency and accountability to a system my 
consƟtuents – and all Virginians – depend on. Aﬀordability and grid modernizaƟon are challenges too big 
for any one enƟty to tackle alone — they require all of us at the table. I and the Energy Commission of 
Virginia remain commiƩed to working with PJM, FERC and other key stakeholders to bring down costs 
and deliver the reliable power Virginians expect. 
Very Truly Yours, 
 
 
 
Senator Scott A. Surovell 
34th District 
Chair, Energy Commission of Virginia
